### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Remark 6.1.2, printed p. 220 (PDF p. 240); item `riehl:6.1:remark2`.

Riehl's clause (a) is exactly this issue's Corollaries 3 and 4, in both handednesses: when the functor one extends along is fully faithful **and** the Kan extension is pointwise, the unit (resp. counit) is a natural isomorphism, so the extension genuinely extends the original functor up to isomorphism. Two points worth carrying into the implementation:

- Riehl makes the **pointwise** hypothesis explicit and demonstrates that it is essential — her Example 6.2.15 exhibits a fully faithful inclusion and a left Kan extension whose unit components are not invertible, precisely because it is not pointwise. So the in-tree statement must carry the pointwise hypothesis rather than deriving invertibility from full faithfulness alone. That counterexample is filed as its own issue in the Riehl Chapter 6 batch.
- Riehl's clause (b) is the converse observation that a strict, on-the-nose extension need not be a Kan extension at all; its witnesses are her Example 6.1.5 (recorded against the group-theoretic induction issue) and Exercise 6.1.iv (in the counterexample issue), so nothing is added to this issue's scope by it.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Example 6.1.4, printed p. 221 (PDF p. 241); item `riehl:6.1:example4`.

This is the case of this issue's second exercise in which the domain is the terminal category: the representable functor on an object, together with the identity at that object, is the left Kan extension of the singleton-valued functor along the corresponding point of the category — i.e. `Lan_K M(m,−) ≅ C(K m,−)` at `M := 1`. The contravariant representable is the same statement applied to the opposite category, so it adds no obligation.

The Riehl verification pass recorded that the mathematical content is already in tree as `Yoneda_Lemma` (`Functor/Hom/Yoneda.v:133`, `∀ A : C, Presheaves [Hom ─,A] F ≅ F A`) and `Covariant_Yoneda_Lemma` (`:182`); only the Kan packaging is missing, and no Kan extension is ever formed along a functor **out of** the terminal category (the tree's only such use is in the opposite direction, along the terminal functor). Cite those two lemmas as the ready ingredients.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) At the terminal-category instance: elements of `F c` correspond to 2-cells filling the triangle, the unique factorization associated with an element is the natural transformation built in the proof of the Yoneda lemma, and the pasting identity is that its component at `c` sends the identity to that element.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Example 6.1.5, printed pp. 221–222 (PDF pp. 241–242); item `riehl:6.1:example5`.

This is the trivial-subgroup case of this issue's adjoint triple: restriction along the unique functor from the terminal category into the delooping, whose left adjoint is the group-indexed coproduct and whose right adjoint the group-indexed product, with unit the coproduct injection and counit the product projection at the identity element. It is what this issue's pointwise formulas give at that shape, and a footnote of Riehl's records that a function of indexing sets induces the corresponding map of products componentwise.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The trivial-subgroup instance stated for an arbitrary target with (co)products, not only for setoids: the left Kan extension is the group-indexed coproduct with unit the injection at the identity element, and the right Kan extension the group-indexed product with counit the projection there.
- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The constant functor giving an object the trivial action is a **strict** extension along that functor, yet — since Kan extensions are unique — it is neither the left nor the right Kan extension unless the group is trivial. This is the library's witness for Riehl's Remark 6.1.2(b), that a strict extension need not be a Kan extension.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Proposition 6.1.6, printed p. 223 (PDF p. 243); item `riehl:6.1:prop6`.

Riehl's proposition is this issue's local-to-global assembly: if the left and right Kan extensions along a functor exist for **every** diagram, then those assignments are respectively a left and a right adjoint to restriction along it, giving the adjoint string. The following was established by the Riehl verification pass and should be carried into the implementation:

- The library **defines** the global Kan extension to be an adjoint of restriction — `Class LeftKan := { Lan : [A,C] ⟶ [B,C]; lan_adjoint : Lan ⊣ Induced }` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:222`) and `Class RightKan := { Ran; ran_adjoint : Induced ⊣ Ran }` (`:140`) over `Induced := (− ◯ F)` (`:127`, whose `fmap` is the whiskering `transform[f] (F z)`, so it is the honest restriction functor). Consequently "restriction has both adjoints" is a definitional field here rather than a theorem.
- Only the **converse** half is proved in tree: `LeftKan_to_LocalLeftKan` (`:249`) and `RightKan_to_LocalRightKan` (`:180`) derive the local universal property from the global adjoint, with the unit defined as the adjunction transpose of the identity. That is Riehl's *following* paragraph (objects in the image of an adjoint to precomposition are Kan extensions), not the proposition.
- The generic machinery for the missing direction exists and is unused: `Theory/Universal/Arrow.v:214` `Definition AdjunctionFromUniversalArrows (H : ∀ c : C, UniversalArrow c U) : @Adjunction _ _ (LeftAdjointFunctorFromUniversalArrows H) U`, over `Class UniversalArrow (c : C) (F : D ⟶ C) := { arrow_initial : @Initial (=(c) ↓ F); … }` (`:127`, with `LeftAdjointFunctorFromUniversalArrows` at `:185`). It is never instantiated at the restriction functor, and no lemma identifies a local Kan extension with a universal arrow into it.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The assembly requires **no** pointwise, smallness or (co)completeness hypothesis: if every local Kan extension along the functor exists, they assemble into the adjoint string. State it at that generality, and prove the identification of a local Kan extension with a universal arrow into the restriction functor so that `AdjunctionFromUniversalArrows` can be instantiated at it.
- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The Kan-extension unit is the component at the diagram of the **assembled** adjunction's unit (dually for the counit), proved as a theorem about the assembled adjoint rather than read off the definition in the converse direction.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Example 6.1.7, printed p. 223 (PDF p. 243); item `riehl:6.1:example7`.

Riehl names induction and coinduction of group representations as the left and right Kan extensions along the delooping of a subgroup inclusion, which is exactly this issue's adjoint triple together with its work item supplying `LeftKan`/`RightKan` instances at that shape — so the Kan identification is already in scope here and no new obligation arises. She also notes that the same discussion applies to group-sets, group-spaces, based group-spaces and group-objects in any category, with the caveat that in a category with few limits or colimits the adjoints need not exist; that caveat is worth recording in the header alongside the (co)completeness hypothesis this issue already carries.

The explicit coset and (co)equalizer formulas Riehl defers to her Example 6.2.9 are filed as their own issue in the Riehl Chapter 6 batch and depend on this one.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Exercise 6.1.i, printed p. 224 (PDF p. 244); item `riehl:6.1:exi`.

The exercise asks for the left and right Kan extensions of a functor along the identity, which is this issue's identity remark. The Riehl verification pass confirmed the negative in detail: `Lan` and `Ran` occur in exactly two files tree-wide and never at the identity; `Induced` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:127`) is never instantiated at the identity functor; and the only ready ingredients are `Theory/Functor.v:304` `fun_equiv_id_right` and `:309` `fun_equiv_id_left`. Note that `Instance/Adjoints.v:42` `adj_id` and `Adjunction/Compose.v:65` `Definition Adjunction_Id {C} : Id[C] ⊣ Id[C] := adj_id` are base-category statements, **not** adjoints of precomposition between functor categories, so they do not discharge this.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The **local** form as well as the global one: for a single diagram, exhibit the local right and left Kan extensions along the identity with identity 2-cell. Riehl's §6.5 uses precisely this local form (together with automatic pointwiseness) to derive the coslice and slice (co)limit formulas for an arbitrary functor.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.1 Exercise 6.1.iii, printed p. 224 (PDF p. 244); item `riehl:6.1:exiii`.

Riehl states the same composition law, but for **left** Kan extensions and as a biconditional: given 2-cells exhibiting one pair as the left Kan extension of a diagram along the first functor, the second pair is the left Kan extension along the second functor if and only if the pasted composite is the left Kan extension along the composite functor.

The Riehl verification pass recorded one concrete work item that this issue's plan does not name: the ingredient identity relating restriction along a composite to the composite of the restrictions is nowhere proved in tree — the restriction functor is never composed with another restriction — and `Adjunction/Compose.v:173` `Definition Adjunction_Compose : (F' ◯ F) ⊣ (U ◯ U')`, while relevant to the global form, makes no Kan claim.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.1) The left-handed dual, both directions of the biconditional, at the **local** level: with one pair exhibiting a left Kan extension along the first functor, the second pair is a left Kan extension along the second functor iff the pasted composite is one along the composite functor.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.2 Theorem 6.2.1 with the numbered displays (6.2.2) and (6.2.3), printed pp. 225–227 (PDF pp. 245–247); item `riehl:6.2:thm1`.

Same theorem, in both handednesses: if the relevant colimits over the comma categories exist then they define the left Kan extension, with the unit extracted as the colimit-cone leg at the identity, and dually for limits and the right Kan extension. Riehl's proof also constructs the action on morphisms from the reindexing functor and proves naturality of the unit before verifying the universal property.

The Riehl verification pass sharpened the in-tree picture and it is worth restating precisely, because the only apparent counterexample to "absent" is weaker than it looks. `Kan_Limit` (`Structure/Limit/Kan/Extension.v:46`, `Lim ≅ Ran (Erase J) F ttt`, `Qed` at `:148`) falls short in four separate ways: it is the single special case where one extends along the terminal functor; it **assumes** a global right Kan extension and merely compares its value with the limit, so none of the existence content of Theorem 6.2.1 is present; it is object-level at the single object of the terminal category, with no comma category, no reindexing functor, no functoriality of the extension and no identification of the counit with a limit-cone leg; and there is no colimit dual anywhere (`ls Structure/Limit/Kan/` shows `Extension.v` alone). `Theory/Kan/Extension.v:74–79` concedes the point in its own header: the comma-category and coend formulas are "a bridge not yet formalized".

The reindexing functor and its projection-compatibility equation — which this issue's functoriality step needs — are filed as their own issue in the Riehl Chapter 6 batch, over `Construction/Comma.v`.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.2 Definition 6.2.6, printed pp. 227–228 (PDF pp. 247–248); item `riehl:6.2:def6`.

Riehl defines pointwise via the (co)limit formula and then proves (her Theorem 6.3.7, this issue's Theorem 3) that it agrees with the representable-preservation definition, so both of this issue's definitions are hers. One detail of her formulation is sharper than a bare object-level isomorphism and should be preserved in the in-tree definition:

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.2) The pointwise condition pins the 2-cell as well as the object: the extension is pointwise when its value at each object is isomorphic to the (co)limit **and** the unit component at each object of the source is the colimit-cone leg at the identity (dually the counit is the limit-cone leg there) — not merely when the objects agree.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.2 Corollary 6.2.7, printed p. 228 (PDF p. 248); item `riehl:6.2:cor7`.

Same existence corollary, in both handednesses: with a small source and a locally small target of the extension, every comma category is small, so cocompleteness (resp. completeness) of the codomain makes all left (resp. right) Kan extensions exist, be pointwise, and assemble into the adjoints of restriction.

The Riehl verification pass left an explicit instruction for whoever implements this, which is worth repeating here because it determines the shape of the work: the **conclusion's adjunction packaging already exists in tree as a definition** — `Class LeftKan := { Lan; lan_adjoint : Lan ⊣ Induced }` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:222`) and `Class RightKan := { Ran; ran_adjoint : Induced ⊣ Ran }` (`:140`) over `Induced` (`:127`) — and **no instance of either class is constructed anywhere in the tree** (both out-of-file occurrences are hypotheses). `Structure/Complete.v:115` `Complete` and `:119` `Cocomplete` exist and are never used to produce a Kan instance. So the work is to *construct* those instances from (co)completeness and to add a pointwise notion; an issue that re-defines the classes would duplicate `Theory/Kan/Extension.v`. Note also that the library has no smallness predicate at all (size is universe-polymorphic), which the verifier explicitly declined to treat as grounds for calling this out of scope — the smallness hypothesis has to be rendered some other way, and how is part of the work.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.2) Record pointwiseness as part of the conclusion: Riehl asserts existence, pointwiseness and the adjunction together, so the constructed instances should come with a proof that the extensions they produce are pointwise.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.2 Corollary 6.2.14, printed p. 231 (PDF p. 251); item `riehl:6.2:cor14`.

Clause (a) is this issue's Corollaries 3 and 4 stated in both handednesses, with the same proof: full faithfulness makes the canonical functor from the slice into the comma category an isomorphism over the source, and the slice has a terminal object, so the (co)limit is computed by evaluating there and the unit is invertible. The in-tree tool for the last step — a (co)limit over an index category with a terminal (resp. initial) object is computed at that object — is filed as #334.

Clause (b) is not in this issue's current scope and is a distinct formalizable consequence:

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.2) Clause (b): when all pointwise left (resp. right) Kan extensions along a fully faithful functor exist, the adjunction with restriction is coreflective (resp. reflective), and in particular the left Kan extension functor is itself fully faithful. Riehl derives this from the invertible-unit criterion filed as #367.

Verification note: the nearest in-tree relative, `Construction/Reflective.v:92` `Lemma reflective_counit_iso … : reflector R (Incl C S x) ≅[Sub C S] x`, is about a full reflective **subcategory inclusion** inside a single category, not about the Kan adjunction between functor categories, and carries no pointwise hypothesis; it asserts neither clause.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.2 Exercise 6.2.ii, printed p. 232 (PDF p. 252); item `riehl:6.2:exii`.

The same two adjoints to the vertex functor, but obtained by a different route: Riehl presents quivers as the set-valued functors on the two-object shape with a parallel pair, so that the vertex functor **is** restriction along the functor from the terminal category that picks out the vertex object, and asks for the adjoints to be computed by the Kan-extension (co)limit formula.

Two notes from the Riehl verification pass. First, the presentations differ: `Construction/Free/Quiver.v` uses the edge-indexed-by-endpoints presentation (`Class Quiver` with `nodes`/`edges`/`edgeset`), whereas Riehl's quivers are functors out of the parallel-pair shape. If the presheaf presentation is introduced, relate it to the existing `QuiverCategory` rather than adding a third notion of quiver. Second, the near miss `Instance/Parallel.v:166` `Program Definition Presheaf_Graph : Parallel^op ⟶ Sets` is a **single object** of that presheaf category (vertices and edges over the naturals), not the category itself, and carries no vertex functor and no adjoints.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.2) Exhibit the vertex functor as restriction along the functor from the terminal category selecting the vertex object, and derive both adjoints from the Kan-extension (co)limit formula (#589) — not only by direct transposition.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Definition 6.3.1, printed p. 232 (PDF p. 252); item `riehl:6.3:def1`.

Riehl's definition is this issue's, stated for **left** Kan extensions: a functor preserves a left Kan extension when the whiskered pair — the composite functor together with the whiskered unit — is again a left Kan extension of the composite diagram. The dual for right Kan extensions is used throughout her §6.3 without separate statement.

The Riehl verification pass confirmed the two weaknesses this issue already identifies, with the precise reasons. `preserves_left_Kan` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:307`) and `preserves_right_Kan` (`:313`) assert only a bare natural isomorphism of the two extending functors, with no mention of the unit; `≈` on functors is `Functor_Setoid` (`Theory/Functor.v:148`), an unconstrained natural isomorphism with no coherence to any unit, so a functor could satisfy the in-tree condition by accident while failing the book's. And both are quantified over the **global** adjoint classes on *both* sides, so preservation of a single local extension — the form Riehl's Definitions 6.3.5 and 6.3.6 require — is not expressible at all; the value of the extension is only projectable from the global class. Both definitions are dead code in tree: their only intended consumer is the abandoned preservation theorem this issue already undertakes to replace.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Lemma 6.3.2, printed pp. 232–233 (PDF pp. 252–253); item `riehl:6.3:lem2`.

Riehl's lemma is the left-handed dual of this issue's Theorem 1, and she gives two proofs: a chain of natural isomorphisms in which the transported identity is identified with the whiskered unit, closing by the Yoneda lemma; and a pasting argument using the unit, the counit and both triangle identities, which exhibits the factorization explicitly and proves it unique.

The Riehl verification pass established the in-tree position exactly. The auxiliary hom-isomorphism of the first proof **is** proved: `left_adjoint_impl` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:328`, `Qed` at `:374`). The lemma itself is not: `left_adjoints_preserve` (`:386`) carries three `admit`s (`:433`, `:435`, `:437`) and ends in `Abort.` at `:438`, so the constant is not in the environment and introduces no axioms — the file's own comment at `:376–384` says so accurately, which is honest disclosure and not a library defect. What is in the environment instead is only the strictly weaker cocontinuity corollary, `left_adjoint_preserves_colimits` (`Adjunction/Continuity.v:223`) and `right_adjoint_preserves_limits` (`:202`) — and Riehl is explicit that this is **not** enough, because it covers only the Kan extensions that happen to be built as (co)limits.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.3) The left-handed statements at the **local** level: preservation of a specified local left Kan extension, and "every left adjoint preserves every left Kan extension" — with the header recording that this is strictly stronger than the cocontinuity corollary, which reaches only the extensions constructed as colimits.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Definition 6.3.5, printed p. 234 (PDF p. 254); item `riehl:6.3:def5`.

Identical to this issue's definition of a pointwise right Kan extension: with a locally small codomain, an extension is pointwise when it is preserved (in the sense of the preservation definition) by every covariant representable on the codomain. No new obligation.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Definition 6.3.6, printed p. 234 (PDF p. 254); item `riehl:6.3:def6`.

Riehl gives the **left-handed** definition, which Mac Lane's §X.5 does not state, and derives it from a duality this issue should record: left and right Kan extensions are dual not under reversing the direction of functors but under reversing the direction of natural transformations, since a functor is equally a functor between the opposite categories while the components of a natural transformation reverse.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.3) The left/dual half: with a locally small codomain, a left Kan extension is pointwise when it is preserved by every **contravariant** representable — equivalently, when it is computed by the colimit formula over the comma category — together with the 2-cell duality that relates the two definitions.

Implementation note from the Riehl verification pass: the 2-categorical opposite is not formalized in tree (`Instance/Cat/Bicategory.v` gives the bicategory structure but no such involution), so the duality has to be stated concretely rather than as a 2-functor. The contravariant representable itself exists as `Functor/Hom.v:146` `Curried_CoHom` (with `Curried_Hom` at `:60`) and is currently connected to nothing in the Kan development.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Theorem 6.3.7, printed pp. 234–235 (PDF pp. 254–255); item `riehl:6.3:thm7`.

Same theorem as this issue's Theorem 3, with both codomain and target of the extension locally small: a right Kan extension is preserved by all covariant representables **iff** it is computed by the limit formula over the comma category — and in that case the limit in particular exists. One direction is immediate because covariant representables preserve limits; the converse chains the Yoneda lemma with the defining universal property through the cone bijection. Riehl states the theorem explicitly as the reconciliation of the representable definition with the earlier (co)limit-formula definition, which is exactly this issue's framing.

The dual, colimit half is recorded as a checkbox on the left-handed pointwise definition (Riehl's Definition 6.3.6), also filed against this issue.

Verification note: the three nearest in-tree relatives were each checked and none asserts this — `Kan_Limit` (`Structure/Limit/Kan/Extension.v:46`) is the terminal-functor special case and the only theorem in that file; `WeightedLimit` (`Structure/Limit/Weighted.v:101`) with `conical_weighted` (`:354`) is proved only for the constant weight; and `right_adjoint_preserves_limits` (`Adjunction/Continuity.v:202`) never exhibits a representable as a right adjoint.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Lemma 6.3.8, printed p. 235 (PDF p. 255); item `riehl:6.3:lem8`.

Identical to this issue's Lemma 1: for locally small categories, cones with a given summit over the composite of the comma projection with the diagram correspond naturally to natural transformations from the hom-functor into the extension direction to the hom-functor into the diagram. Riehl's proof reads a cone as a choice, for each map into the image, of a morphism in the codomain, and shows the cone condition is exactly the naturality square.

Implementation guidance from the Riehl verification pass, which found the right-hand side already present as vocabulary: `Structure/Limit/Weighted.v:49`'s `HomDiagram c F` **is** the functor sending an object to the hom-setoid into the diagram, and the `WeightedLimit` class (`:101`) is stated through the setoid of natural transformations from a weight into it — that is, the shape of Riehl's right-hand side already exists. What is missing is any instance or theorem taking the weight to be the hom-functor into the image, and the diagram formed by composing the comma projection with the diagram, which appears nowhere. State this lemma as a weighted-limit instance at that weight rather than building a parallel cone notion. The other two near misses are genuinely different: `Cone_Natural_Transform`/`Cone_Comma` (`Structure/Cone/Const.v:53`, `:72`) and `Cones_Comma` (`Instance/Cones/Comma.v`) classify cones by the **constant** weight and by the comma of the diagonal in the functor category.

Riehl also notes that when the source is not small the comma category is not small either, so a priori there may be more than a set's worth of cones, and that the isomorphisms of her Theorem 6.3.7 show the collections are in fact sets. In this library sizes are universe-polymorphic, so the point should be recorded in the header rather than tracked as a separate obligation.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3 Exercise 6.3.i, printed p. 236 (PDF p. 256); item `riehl:6.3:exi`.

A corollary of this issue's pointwise definition, on the copower side, which is not currently in its scope:

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.3) If the codomain is locally small and has all small copowers, then **every** right Kan extension into it is pointwise; dually, with all small powers, every left Kan extension into it is pointwise. (Requires copowers, #321, on which this issue already depends.)

Verification note: `rg -i 'copower|cotensor|tensoring by a set'` returns 0 relevant hits in tree, and every `power` hit is unrelated — the finite powers of `Theory/Multicategory/Endomorphism.v`, the Lawvere object powers, the topos power object, and an author's surname. `Adjunction/SAFT.v:161`'s `cogen_power` is an ad-hoc hom-indexed product built for the special adjoint functor theorem, not a general copower; `Structure/Limit/Product.v`'s `iprod` could express one, but no abbreviation is defined.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.3, the boldfaced unnumbered construction, printed p. 236 (PDF p. 256); item `riehl:6.3:construction-cone-category`.

The same cone and cocone shapes as this issue's Exercise 3.6.vi, defined the same way: the cone under a small category is the pushout, in the category of categories, of the inclusion of one end of the cylinder along the unique functor to the terminal category, which collapses that end to a single freely adjoined terminal object and adds nothing else; the dual pushout along the other inclusion adjoins an initial object. Riehl restates it in §6.3 because it is the indexing shape for her characterisation of (co)completeness as an adjointness, which is filed as its own issue in the Riehl Chapter 6 batch and depends on this one.

Verification note supporting this issue's work item 1: `ls Instance/Cat/*.v` is exactly `Bicategory.v`, `Cartesian.v`, `Cocartesian.v`, and the `Cocartesian` file is binary **coproducts** of categories, not pushouts — so the ambient pushout machinery the construction presupposes is genuinely part of this issue's scope and not available elsewhere.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.4, the boldfaced definition in running prose, printed p. 241 (PDF p. 261); item `riehl:6.4:def-absolute-kan-extension`.

Riehl's definition is this issue's: a Kan extension is **absolute** when it is preserved not merely by representables — which is pointwiseness — but by **all** functors out of its codomain, so absoluteness strictly strengthens pointwiseness. She uses it for the derived-functor propositions of §6.4, which are filed separately in the Riehl Chapter 6 batch and depend on this issue.

The Riehl verification pass mapped the in-tree situation precisely, and the two halves exist separately and never meet. `functor_preserves_split` (`Structure/Coequalizer/Split.v:104`, `SplitCoequalizer f g → SplitCoequalizer (fmap[F] f) (fmap[F] g)`, under the header "Absoluteness: every functor preserves split coequalizers" at `:98`) supplies the absoluteness **quantifier**, but only for split coequalizers, and is never identified with a Kan extension — and since the in-tree limit/Kan bridge `Kan_Limit` is stated only for limits and right Kan extensions, with its colimit dual appearing only as prose, the absolute split coequalizer is never exhibited as an absolute left Kan extension. Conversely `preserves_right_Kan` (`Theory/Kan/Extension.v:313`) is about Kan extensions but has the quantifiers **inverted** relative to absoluteness: it fixes a functor and quantifies over all extensions, and demands the extension exist globally on both sides, so it cannot express "this extension is absolute". There is no per-extension preservation predicate for the local Kan classes at all.

- [ ] (from Riehl §6.4) State absoluteness for **left** Kan extensions as well as right, and record the comparison Riehl draws — absolute implies pointwise, strictly — as a proved implication once the pointwise notion (#599) is available.

### Also covered by

Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*, 2nd ed., §6.5 Proposition 6.5.1, printed p. 242 (PDF p. 262); item `riehl:6.5:prop1`.

Same statement as this issue's Theorem 1, in both handednesses and with the existence biconditional Riehl states outright ("one exists if and only if the other does"). Her proof also identifies the colimit cocone with the Kan unit: composing an object of the target with the terminal functor gives the constant diagram, so the universal property of the extension says exactly that cocones under the diagram correspond to morphisms out of the extension's value.

The Riehl verification pass confirmed the three shortfalls this issue undertakes to fix and added a fourth worth recording: besides being limit-only, non-biconditional and object-level (the cone is built inside the proof of `Kan_Limit` at `Structure/Limit/Kan/Extension.v:49` and only the apex objects are compared), the hypothesis is the **global** right Kan class — a right adjoint to precomposition on the whole functor category, i.e. completeness of the codomain for that shape — rather than the local right Kan extension of the single diagram that the proposition is about, even though the local class is defined at `Theory/Kan/Extension.v:154`.

### Also covered by
